utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand or that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you and good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers for the Office of the Prosecution. With me today are co-counsel Ms. Joanne Richardson, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, and Mr. Jose Doria. Our case manager is Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and good morning to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning to the Defence also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us this morning our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, as well as Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. I'm still wondering and this keeps haunting me. Each Defence team has basically four members, no? It's lead counsel, co-counsel, legal assistant and case manager. I'm just wondering how this courtroom can take -- can take six teams. There are some sections which can take four persons but I still don't understand. The same with -- and where will be the case manager and the co-counsel and the legal assistant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It troubles me. So any preliminaries before I give the floor to Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no preliminaries from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries from your side, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you don't have to ask us, "Lend me your ears," because we are all ears already. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a great responsibility to address the Honourable Chamber with closing arguments after a 16-month trial. There is so much at stake. At the start of the trial, we asked the Honourable Chamber to examine the facts only and to distinguish between the myth and reality, and at the end of the trial, to render a just judgement. We are now at the stage when the Honourable Chamber will withdraw for deliberations. Again, we seek only justice from you. The Defence is not seeking for an acquittal under the influence of factors that are beyond this case file. The facts of the case speak clearly enough in the favour of such a judgement, of such a verdict. The Honourable Chambers knows, is aware, that the judgement in this case will not be rendered on the basis of whether the people in Srebrenica suffered or not. Instead, you will subject the evidence to close scrutiny in order to arrive at the answers to the following questions: Where it is proved that some crimes alleged in the indictment were indeed committed, were some of the perpetrators subordinated to the accused? Did the accused know of the crimes committed by his subordinates? Did the accused fail to take the necessary and reasonable measures in order to deal with these crimes? And, in connection with Article 7(1) of the charge for wanton destruction, did the accused deliberately apply the policy of torching, as a means of warfare, as the Prosecutor indeed asserted? You will find that all these questions have only one answer: No. At different stages of the trial, the Honourable Chamber announced that they will emotionally disassociate themselves in approaching this case and that they will approach it with surgical precision. We are glad that this is the case because we did not expect anything else. The metaphor of surgical precision is indeed appropriate for this case. If the scalpel of justice is well handled, justice will have been satisfied. If it is used wrongly, it will make irreparable damage. The approach of the Prosecution in this case was all but surgical. It was generalised, vague, ambiguous and contradictory from the very start, the reason being that the case was misconceived. The case is unfounded. It is only with the assistance of ploys, mistaken meanings, misunderstood words, misinterpretation of documents, that only an appearance of a genuine case can be made. Their case is, as we said at the start, a hall of mirrors. It is a house of cards made out of different decks. Since the Honourable Chamber will approach the facts of the case with surgical precision, you will not confuse testimonies as did the Prosecution in their final brief, as we have stressed several times in our reply to this brief. You will not confuse time periods as they did. You will not conceal considerable differences, as the Prosecution did, differences between fighters and civilians, between fighters and those who torched houses, between perpetrators of crimes and prison guards, between the War Presidency and staff, between the TO structure and the corps structure. These, Your Honours, are only some of the examples of such differences that the Prosecution was not willing to clarify. Moreover, the Honourable Chamber will not apply the legal theory whereby the accused is held responsible for every evil that befell anyone in Srebrenica in the course of 1992 and 1993. My colleague will address you on legal matters tomorrow, and I shall say only the following of this topic. The Honourable Chamber will not convict the accused for cruel treatment or murder because people were killed or because they were cruelly treated in Srebrenica, if the Honourable Chamber finds that this was indeed the case. Only if a direct and specific nexus is found with the accused and through his subordinates, as well as his specific knowledge of their crimes, the Honourable Chamber will be able to do that. The evidence of the case does not support such findings at any rate. At the very start of this case, of this trial, we described the hell in Srebrenica in the course of 1992 and 1993 in using four words: Genocide, siege, starvation, and disease. We believe that the Honourable Chamber realised the situation even if the Prosecution did not. At the end of the Prosecution case, you announced that you accepted the fact that Srebrenica was under siege and that it was confronted with starvation during the relevant time period. It faced not only starvation, Your Honours, but the daily threat of terrible massacres by Serbs were the defence lines to fall. What happened in July 1995 might have happened also in December 1992, in January 1993, in February 1993, at any point in time. The people living there were with their backs to the wall and the only possibility they had was to flee below the ground. These people were aware of that. The greatest mistake one can make in describing the situation is to consider it to be merely a background, as if starvation, a refugee crisis and disease are only scenery, scenery behind the stage, immovable, whilst actors tread the stage. Were this the case, the scenery might well be ignored. The facts of the case could be analysed individually and the siege and death from shells would merely be pale scenery and would ultimately be considered irrelevant for the case. This is not even remotely the truth. Since this is command responsibility that is relevant here, the military and humanitarian situation are closely related with every single fact in this case. In order to understand this, the appropriate analogy would be that of a football match which is brought to a stop by a mob of football supporters who run up into the football field. No one would pretend that this football match can be analysed by simply ignoring the fact that hundreds of people ran up to the football field in the middle of a match. One could hardly find fault with the players for playing badly or for being an off-side when the match itself turned into mayhem, into torching of tear gas with enraged people. In total chaos. But change the scenery of this particular scene. Imagine this football match being that of fighters with scarce weaponry. Take their uniforms off. Imagine that they are exposed to deadly shells. Imagine that they are starved and that they have been under siege for weeks. Imagine that they are running uphill and trying to confront a well-trained and armed enemy. Imagine thousands of distraught civilians among them. Now you will have the picture of what the fighting in Srebrenica in 1992 was like. Out of this metaphor, you were able to see that it will be ridiculous to take these facts merely as a background. The background is a moving picture which has form and movement. It has to be regarded as a phenomenon. Appropriate questions must be asked. Why did the mob occupy the football team -- the football field? And in our case, why did thousands of civilians go into action to get hold of food? Because they were dying of hunger. And why were they dying of hunger? Because the Serbs chased them away from their homes and then held them under siege. Who held them under siege? Serbs from the surrounding villages. Which villages? The ones that were attacked, the ones that were mentioned and alleged in the indictment. Which Serbs? The villagers of Rakovica, Jezestica, Fakovici, Bjelovac and Kravica. Many of the witnesses in this case. Why didn't the fighters have uniforms? Because it wasn't an army. These were citizens responding to an attack. Why did they have so few weapons, mostly hunting rifles? Because that was all that they had at the time the Serb army attacked them in their homes. Your Honours, every fact in this case is directly and specifically connected with the ethnic cleansing by Serbs and the humanitarian catastrophe that was the result of the ethnic cleansing. The phenomenon of a soldier/citizen or levee en masse, lack of communications. Where the accused was depended on where a deathly threat had to be confronted. These facts cannot be separated from the ethnic cleansing of eastern Bosnia. Every single fact in this case is a result of that. Your Honour, this also applies to the credibility of Serb witnesses. The Honourable Chamber understood the situation in Srebrenica describing it as hell on earth in its decision dated 4th of July, 2005, the findings case -- decision. You referred to the siege of Srebrenica and the enormous military predominance of Serbs. What, then, of the credibility of Serb witnesses who came here and denied all that? It has to be and is disrupted by the fact that they refused to acknowledge the reality. In our final brief we spoke about the invisible arm which, in the submission of the Prosecution, must have held Srebrenica under siege. Truth be told, they call it the so-called siege of Srebrenica. Your Honours, you accepted that Srebrenica was under siege but not so the Prosecution. This tells a lot of their realism and of their approach to the people of Srebrenica, whose suffering under siege they don't even wish to mention. You remember the words from the book of Larry Hollingworth, D218. In this book he described how the Serb army, and I quote: "Persecuted innocent women and children from village to village until they were finally chased away to Srebrenica, a place where one had no where to flee from, and where their destiny was to be transported as cattle and slaughtered as lambs." Echoing this situation was their own witness, Colonel Tucker, who they referred to frequently in their final -- in their closing arguments, and I quote: "The issue for the refugees in Srebrenica, for those who surrounded us, was that they believed that they would die. The question was not whether they would die. The question was only when they would die." And that's his testimony on the 15th of March 2005, transcript pages 5959 to 5960. The ambassador, Diego Arria, described the situation in Srebrenica that he experienced as the slow-motion genocide. That is the way UN documents described it. I refer you to D956. For the Prosecution, the ethnic cleansing of eastern Bosnia and the military predominance of Serbs seemed to have existed in a parallel dimension, as if in some other parallel dimension there existed camps set up pursuant to the order of the Serbian government of Birac on the moving out of the Muslim population. As you know, the area of Srebrenica was part of Birac. As you know, Your Honours, you saw this order in D731 and you know that this was organised and ordered. Edina Karic told a touching story about this in her testimony on the 14th of September, 2005, transcript pages 11037, 11039. On these camps and persecutions, their own witness, Ibrahim Becirevic, spoke in detail, and I refer to the transcript dated 25 April 2005, page 7617. Many others spoke of this. The reality, in essence, is very simple and the procedure of placing an area under siege is easily understandable. The Serbs first chased away all the Muslims from the surrounding areas. The areas can be seen on the map. You can see the map now; it's D705. We are well familiar with their names now. The Muslims were chased away from Podrinje along the Drina east of Srebrenica, from the north of the Bratunac area to the west of Srebrenica, from Vlasenica, Milici, Han Pijesak and to the south from the area of Skelani. Srebrenica was surrounded and cut off from the rest of the world. After that, food supplies were interdicted in order to starve the population. They achieved this easily by controlling the main roads. It was only the American food packages in the air drops in February 1993 that somewhat hindered Serbs in their intentions. The fact that it was necessary to drop packages from the air perfectly illustrates that the only way to reach Srebrenica was vertically, from the air. Unfortunately the residents of Srebrenica did not have wings. Luckily for them the Americans did. In the course of 1992, the people in Srebrenica were completely cut off and desperately hungry. They ate berries and grounded acorns -- and ground acorns in order to make bread. They lived like animals under open air in woods, and the Serbs shelled and fired upon them, as if they had been beasts. In what way was the siege maintained? Around every single Serb village, including Ratkovici, Fakovici, Bjelovac, Jezestica and Kravica minefields were laid. There was patrolling and shells were fired upon the places where there were Muslims, be it villages or woods. In this way, Muslims were held like sheep in a fold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I am not receiving interpretation, unless there is a delay. I notice I think that -- yes. There has been a switch between interpreters. Would you mind, Ms. Vidovic, repeating your last two sentences? Basically that's what we have missed. I'm sorry to have interrupted you like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It will be my pleasure. The Prosecution claims that the local Serbs were peace-loving and that they were only defending themselves. In a way, Your Honours, they were indeed defending themselves. The Serbs were in their villages, surrounded by their minefields, with their guns and artillery, and they really could believe that they were only defending themselves. But if one besieges a people, cutting off their food supply, and on top of that you keep shelling them, you're doing something incredibly violent, threatening their very lives. Whilst those who lay the siege wait for the enemy to starve to death, they indeed have this attitude of defending themselves but nonetheless a lethal one. Those besieged, starving, have to attack in order to get some food, ammunition, and medication to call [Realtime transcript read in error "kill"] those who were besieged to be attackers and to call them who lay the siege the defenders [call not kill] Shouldn't fool anyone apart from a person who is completely wrong about the situation. I will correct for the transcript, Your Honour. To call those who were besieged attackers and to call those who lay the siege defenders shouldn't fool anyone apart from those people who are blatantly wrong. The localities in the indictment were of no marginal importance for the siege of Srebrenica and the Muslim villages of the area. They were the siege. Mr. Ramic, in his testimony of the 28th of August, 2005, on page 9915 of the transcript, described the suffering of the expelled Muslim population in a forest called Poljana, in the area of Poznanovici. The suffering of thousands of people in the open, including women, children and the elderly. He described that they were attacked by the Serb forces from Ratkovici. He described the daily shelling of the Muslim villages of Mocevici, Dedici, Podkorjen, from Ratkovici, during June of 1992. Witness Tiro described the very same. On the 5th of September, 2005, he described the attack on Orlica, and he identified the attackers as people being from Grabovacka Rijeka and Fakovici. When they left, they left the wasteland and death. They killed every captured Muslim. The testimonies and other evidence mentioning the killings by the people from Fakovici are distressing. Please recall the story of the Serb soldier Slobodan Misic and his statement to a journalist. It was D832. He described the murders of Muslims around Fakovici, specifically in the village of Tegare. And you should also recall that Misic received his salary for August 1992 as a fighter from the Fakovici unit. You should also bear in mind the document of the Drina Corps which is the report of the 14th of September, 1992, confirming that Tegare were liberated in entirety. That was D966. Could we please see slide number 3 now? Suad Smajlovic testified on the horrific scenes of murders in Tegare that he learned of. He testified on the 6th of December, 2005, page 14483 of the transcript. Ibro Alic testified on the same topic as well on the 17th of October, 2005, transcript page 12542. Both these witnesses confirmed that the killers came from Fakovici. An eyewitness n his testimony on the 3rd of October, 2005, transcript page 11800, described that the Serb soldiers from Jezestica and Kravica set on fire a house in Velika Glogova in which there was a little boy, and on the same day they killed 12 elderly people and women who were unable to flee the Muslim village of Adzici in June 1992. He identified Nedjo Nikolic, aka Djedura from Jezestica as one of the key figures in the attack on Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992. He identified commander Najdan Mladjenovic from the nearby Serb village of Hranca who issued orders to kill. He identified many of his neighbours from Kravica and Jezestica who brutally killed around 65 people in a single day. And Najdan Mladjenovic, Your Honours, the very same Najdan Mladjenovic who, on Prosecution's behalf in this case, identified the allegedly torched Serb houses of that area, and one can find that in P487. We also heard a distressing testimony of Edina Karic, the then 15-year-old girl. She was raped, inter alia, by the Serb soldiers from Bjelovac. She had identified them many years before this case, when she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please proceed, and my apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She had identified them many years prior to this trial, when she provided the first statement you saw. She Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had identified them on the payroll lists of the Territorial Defence of Bjelovac in D83. She identified many local Serbs from Bjelovac, Sase and Pobrdje who ran the camp of Gradina where they killed and tortured people as well as raped little girls. She testified on the 14th of September, 2005, transcript page 11037 to 11042. The siege of Srebrenica and the Muslim villages of the area was not put in place by an invisible hand. It was put in place by the local Serbs. Closely knit and well organised units of the Serb army. And many Prosecution witnesses in this case were also participants of the siege. Mladen Simic, Dragan Djuric, Slavisa Eric, Stanisa and Milenko Stevanovic, Milo Rankovic, Slavoljub Rankic, Slavoljub Filipovic, Nikola Petrovic, Nikola Popovic, Slavoljub Zikic, Dragomir Miladinovic. Evidence shows that they were members of the local Serb army units who lay the siege of Srebrenica. This is important as to their credibility, and it is also important for the issue of military necessity. Your Honours, I wanted to talk about the military necessity itself. At the end of the Prosecution case, Your Honours accepted that the actions mentioned in the indictment had to be undertaken in order to gain food, ammunition and medication. Both Prosecution and Defence may agree on only one thing in this case, and that is precisely this: Additional Protocol I sets out the criteria for what a military target indeed is, or a military objective. In Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, we can read the following: "Attacks shall be limited strictly to military objectives. In so far as objects are concerned, military objectives are limited to those objects which, by their nature, location, purpose or use make an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction capture or neutralisation in the circumstances ruling at the time offers a definite military advantage." Your Honours, by going to the localities mentioned in the indictment and capturing them resulted in clear military advantage. The seizure of food, ammunition, weapons, and medication helped those besieged to survive for another couple of days. The Serbs shelled Muslims from the places mentioned in the indictment, thus killing and mutilating. Therefore, to neutralise such objectives resulted in a clear military advantage. By not allowing the enemy to use those locations, key for the siege of Srebrenica and its villages, indeed represented a clear military advantage, as well as to neutralise the trenches and positions of the artillery. Evidence confirms that the soldiers lived in the houses of the Serb villages and locations. Even in the houses where women and children stayed, there were shells and guns. I will remind you of a Drina Corps document, D723. It is a combat report stating that on the 4th of November, 1992, a five-year-old boy, in the village of Brezovica, was killed during his play with an anti-aircraft gun. The safety was off and it fired accidentally. Your Honours, in the Serb villages around Srebrenica, even little children played with such weaponry. There was a boy playing with an anti-aircraft gun. Your Honours, a correction for the transcript. We provided the speech to the interpreters. I said that in the houses where there were women and children, there were shells, grenades and guns. During those actions, the soldiers used the houses to fire from. Whether Prosecution likes it or not, the absolute military reality is that if a soldier is firing from a house trying to kill you, you are entitled to return fire, and should the fire be -- should the house be set on fire due to the activity of the weapon, for example, a grenade or a hand-held rocket launcher, that's the reality of war. It would be insane to claim that a fighter who -- should try in any which way possible to cause any damage to property when fighting for his life. Your Honours, please recall the Drina Corps document ordering that, from the territories of the Serb villages, Srebrenica was to be attacked. To put forth such silly assertions that -- such as ones that no army in the world wouldn't and couldn't abide by is not in the interests of international humanitarian law. The only consequence of such assertions is the loss of reputation enjoyed by international law in general. In our final brief, we cited in detail and explained why each of the actions undertaken was directed against the legitimate military objectives. The next question is whether during those attacks there was damage caused and -- that wasn't collateral. This is the area in which the Trial Chamber should exercise great care, because if the Chamber wouldn't be careful, it will inadvertently transfer the burden of proof to Defence. Prosecution claims that in each of the attacks, there was damage of property and in a widespread manner. If this is indeed so, the Chamber will have to make their own conclusion but not using this general approach as Prosecution would want you to. You will have to go into a detailed analysis of evidence. You will have to determine what the Prosecutor indeed managed to prove was damaged by fire on the day of the action and by whom. This Chamber knows that it was impossible for Defence to put forth details for each house, whether there were grenades or guns in those houses, or whether those were simply houses that represent collateral damage during legitimate attacks. It would be unjust by the Chamber to -- not to ask Prosecution to prove that each of the houses was wantonly destroyed, but to demand from Defence to prove the opposite, that indeed, it wasn't destroyed wantonly. Defence managed to show that each of the actions pertained in the villages where there was lots of weaponry in a small locality, that there was fierce fighting, that the Serbs went in counter-attacks with the support of their artillery as well as subsequent counter-attacks in order to regain control over those villages with their artillery support. In certain cases, you will recall, I believe, even Serb planes were used. It was on Prosecution to prove that such damage to property wasn't accidental during legitimate attacks because of the fierce fighting, because of the Serb counter-attacks with the artillery backing, and bombs from planes. It was on Prosecution to prove that the houses were destroyed wantonly and that this cannot be considered collateral damage. It is not up to Defence to prove that. When studying the evidence about how property was damaged during those actions, you will have to bear in mind countless ways to cause damage to property during wartime. Let us pause here for a moment to go back to reality. If one is to look at the photographs from the Second World War, you will see what the consequences of warfare were and what sort of damage they caused. To suppose that any property damage caused wantonly, is caused wantonly is not only shifting the burden of proof to Defence but also it means to ignore the horrific reality of war and the reality of the damage that can be caused by heavy artillery and fire-power, particularly in small settlements in which houses were built of inflammable material such as wood. Your Honours, I will now move on to say something about torching by "torbari," the bag people or baggers. In the allegations relating to wanton destruction, the Prosecution alleges not only that every damage to property that resulted from fierce fighting was certainly unnecessary. They also assume that all this unnecessary damage to property was caused by subordinates of the accused rather than by some of the hundreds or thousands civilians carrying bags who, as the Prosecution itself proves, were present in every action and entered houses searching for food. How does this assumption work? We invite the Chamber to go back a step and consider how the Prosecution can ask Your Honours to assume such a thing, to assume that it was precisely the subordinates of the accused who caused the damage. There is simply no evidence to show this. The Prosecution case looks like this: They allege that there is evidence showing that certain units participated in every action. This evidence must be studied thoroughly. I will later explain why. The Prosecution claims, for example, that the Srebrenica TO, the Potocari TO, Suceska TO, Kragljivoda TO, Osmace TO, Skenderovici and Birac TO participated in the action in Fakovici. They allege that these TO units were under the effective control of the accused during the action. According to the allegations of the Prosecution, it must have been them who caused all the wanton damage caused during this action. The fatal flaw in these allegations is that even if these TO units did participate in the action in Fakovici, for example, they were not the only ones. There were thousands of civilians who flocked among the fighters like ants. You will recall the testimony of Prosecution witness Slavoljub Zikic about this, and Your Honours can see the slide now. He describes the fighting on the 5th of October, 1992 in Fakovici. "Question: Is it not true that on that day, there were hundreds of civilians in your village, men, women and children, running around grabbing food and so on? "Answer: It's true. The number was even larger, judging by everything that was taken away from the village on that day. I think it would be difficult for a civilised nation to understand what I'm telling you. In addition to shooting, people are banging on some cans and they were killing dogs. It was seething from all sides, all over the place. There was a lot of noise, and God knows what was being done. I don't think this is something you would find easy to understand, coming from a civilised nation as you do. "Question: Mr. Zikic, isn't it true that with all these people and all this going on, these people were completely out of control? "Answer: It's my opinion that it was indeed out of control. "Question: You told us that they took livestock. You mentioned wheat was taken from your brother. Isn't it right that these people were desperate for food? "Answer: Yes. I understand that fully. There was not a single chicken left in any of the villages. They had all been released. If they had been pent up, well, okay, but there was not a chicken to be seen anywhere around for miles. Therefore, there were many people doing that. "Question: In this scene of absolute pandemonium, the scene of people running around grabbing chickens, no one, no army, could have stopped them from doing what they wanted to do, from getting food. Is that what you accept? "Answer: Yes." Mr. Zikic, a Serb, whose house was burned down and who testified about how he was beaten had no reason to exaggerate when he described the chaos he had seen on that day. He was describing a scene which a civilised people would find difficult to understand. Another Prosecution witness, Dr. Mujkanovic, also wanted to say that we, sitting here in The Hague, in the year 2006, would find it very hard to understand thousands of civilians risking their lives, running where there was shooting and shelling in order to try to obtain food for themselves and their starving children. There is a slide, Your Honour, Dr. Mujkanovic. His response was: "It is a phenomenon that nobody who hasn't experienced it can understand, and it's very hard to explain. Sometimes civilians would enter these villages even before the troops, and sometimes many of them were wounded, many of them were killed, many of them did not accomplish their mission. They didn't get hold of the food, although it was food they came for in the first place." But you must understand this, Your Honours. I invite you to imagine a scene out of hell, thousands of civilians, men, women and children, banging pots and pans, making a terrible noise and running into every house searching for food. Had you been observing this from a hilltop, would you have been able to say, "This house was set on fire by a civilian. That one by a fighter, that one by a 14-year-old boy, this one was damaged by a hand-held rocket launcher, the other one was set fire to by a shell"? Of course, you couldn't have done that. No eyewitness even attempted to make such a list. In view of the fact that uniforms meant nothing in Srebrenica, as Prosecution witness Dr. Mujkanovic stated, no one would have been able to tell whether it was a fighter or somebody else who set fire to a house. Furthermore, not a single witness provided evidence that it was fighters who set fire to houses in any action, especially no one testified that members of, for example, the Skenderovici TO torched a house during an action, or members of the Osmace TO, or of any other TO. In fact, the evidence shows the very opposite. Mujkanovic testified that it was civilians, not fighters, who torched houses. This is the Prosecution evidence on which the Defence relied when deciding what evidence to present during the Defence case. We reminded Your Honours, more than once, on the fantasies of the Office of the Prosecutor who imagined they could call a witness and then ask the Chamber not to believe that witness. That is not a serious approach to a criminal trial. That is a Kafkaesque idea, and we know that Your Honours will not tolerate it for a single second. According to the alternative Prosecution case, allegedly armbands were used to distinguish fighters from civilians. The Prosecution alleges that fighters wore armbands, but has a single Prosecution witness stated that someone wearing an arm band torched his house? No. There is no evidence that a single fighter torched a single house during the actions, not to mention any of the members of any of the Territorial Defence witnesses -- Defence -- Territorial Defence units. This is a fatal flaw in the Prosecution case. If Your Honours establish that there was burning of Serbian villages but that this was done by civilians, then Your Honours will have to find that the accused is not guilty. What is at stake here is not allowing the accused to avoid justice; what is at stake here is the application of law. Perhaps civilians did irresponsibly torch houses because they were furious since they themselves had been expelled from their homes and had lost their homes. In some cases we heard the reasons for this. They were sometimes very painful. They did this because they wanted the war to end. A female witness, a mother, testifying about the reasons why her 12-year-old boy set fire to a house in Kravica said, "I, as a mother, did not want, nobody wanted, to set fire to somebody else's home. The people of Srebrenica, and I think everyone thought the same, we wanted to make our situation easier, to make our life easier. It would have been better when the Serbs left for the refugees to move in there. Even my son did not really want to set fire to the house. He said he torched it because he wanted the evil to end. He wanted the war to end." You heard this testimony on the 31st of August, 2005, transcript pages 10104 to 10105. Unfortunately, Your Honours, such things happened. But to consider the accused responsible for the irresponsible actions of others with which he has nothing to do will not assist to put such actions right. It would only increase the injustice and the misery and the overall human suffering. In its closing speech, the Prosecution claimed that soldiers aided and abetted the torching by civilians. However, this has not been proved by any means. Once again, what the Prosecutor should have proved is that it was Oric's subordinates who caused wanton destruction. However, this has not been proved. On the contrary, what has been proved is that the fighters tried to stop the civilians from going to places where there was fighting. We heard testimony about this from witness Tiro Hamed on the 6th of September, 2005, transcript page 10362. We heard detailed testimony about this from Suad Smajlovic on the 7th of December, 2005, transcript page 14570. And he, Your Honours, was wounded while trying to prevent civilians from entering the battlefield in the Kunjerac area. He described the death of a brave fighter who also attempted to prevent the entry of civilians into the dangerous battlefield. The existence of an understanding between fighters and civilians to destroy villages as mentioned in the indictment is a fiction fabricated by the Office of the Prosecutor without any grounds whatsoever. The only evidence about the attitude of the accused toward the torching of property is what we heard during these proceedings. The only piece of evidence we heard about the accused's attitude to the burning shows that he opposed it vehemently. And this was heard from an OTP witness, Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic. You have a slide, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The testimony of Prosecution witness Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic: "Question: And what was the opinion of Naser Oric in that regard? "Answer: He had had the same opinion. He was against people burning houses but there was simply nothing that he could do. He did not have a way of stopping them. It's not that he simply didn't approve. He fiercely opposed this, but you must know that there were between 80.000 and 100.000 people living in the area. You couldn't keep all these people at bay. It's that simple." Could we now see slide number 8, please? Dr. Mujkanovic again, the 16th of February, 2005. "Question: Finally, as far as you're aware, with your contacts with Naser Oric, he never encouraged these practices? Never encouraged burning or looting? "Answer: I've already confirmed that in my testimony. I said that not only did he not encourage, he saw it as a problem that was a constant subject of discussion at the War Presidency. Naser Oric's position was that there shouldn't be any fires set to property, but nobody could prevent that." Your Honours, many times during the trial, and in its closing arguments, and its final brief, the Prosecution referred to the interview with the accused in order to try to prove certain issues when it suited them. They did not draw your attention to what did not suit their case. They usually said that he was evading the truth; for example, in connection with the protection of property. In the part of his interview, P329, on tape 20, page 21 in the English version, he describes the scene of battle as follows: "While we are fighting here in these trenches which were full, you see it was like this. There was a slope and, down there, there would be a plain, and we wouldn't have taken half of it. The rest would still remain. I would already see the civilians swarming into the village. Explain to me how could I have control over what was happening among the houses? If there is an expert anywhere in the world who can explain to me how I could do it, let him explain it to me at once." And then he goes on to say: "Take into consideration the configuration of the terrain and the area that was supposed to be attacked. The Chetnik firing lines. You now have to consider how many troops I would need with weapons. To stand there without weapons, to link up into a cordon and to tell the civilians, Don't go there, but there is war here at the line, bullets fly here and there. You can't fire every bullet into the air. What fool would stand in a cordon holding his hands like there with bullets flying behind his back and whizzing by? No one. But bear in mind that there was cannibalism there. Elderly people were dying. They were starving to death. There was no machinery that could help somebody carry this out. If there is anyone in this world who can tell me that, how it can be done, then let them lock me up at once for 300 years. Let them shoot me. It was impossible. It was chaos." This is what Naser Oric said to the OTP. Your Honours, the law does not impose on anyone to do the impossible. The Prosecution never advanced a serious suggestion as to how property could be protected from the civilians in this mountainous area, the civilians who risked their lives to get hold of the property. Was the accused supposed to kill civilians to prevent them from coming close to the Serb property? Was property more valuable than human lives? The Prosecution did not find it enough to merely accuse the accused of not having prevented torching. They had to say what he could have done. They had to show that what they think he could have done was feasible. They were supposed to show that. But they didn't. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, as for the other requirement of command responsibility, knowledge, there is no evidence indicating that the accused knew of wanton destruction of property by his subordinates. Now, Your Honours, the fact of the matter here is whether the accused had information about wanton destruction by his own subordinates, not civilians, and not just anyone. In the Prosecution reply to our final brief, for instance, in paragraph 63, the OTP refers to interview P329, tape 20, page 18, that Oric had received reports about the attack on Jezestica and that he extensively discussed that. Actually, it is quite unfortunate that the Prosecution should use precisely this part of the interview. Your Honour, this part of the interview in fact demonstrates the entire lack of professionalism on the part of the investigators and it shows their aggressiveness, which is evident throughout the interview and which went too far in certain places. This is what his reply on the allegedly received report about Jezestica is like. Could we have slide number 9, please, P329, tape 20, page 17. "He was improvising this attack to relieve the pressure on Nurif; what happened in Jezestica as a result of these combat operations, I don't know. "Later, later they told me, they told me that what happened, that they had taken the line very easily and they had taken the attack line very easily and captured quite a lot of weapons." The question by the investigator: "Was this report done orally or on paper?" Naser Oric: "This was not a report; you're immediately trying to tie this up with this and say that it was a report." Investigator: "I'm asking if it was a report." Naser Oric's answer: "No, it wasn't." Investigator's question: "The question was did you receive it orally or in writing?" Your Honours, it is quite clear that the accused is telling the investigators that he had not received a report, and they are asking him, imagine, please, whether he received the report orally or in writing. Far from it. Oric never said that he received a report on the destruction of property. This fraction of the interview demonstrates the way in which the Prosecution arrived at answers to their questions. Such a method of interrogation violates the fundamental principles of criminal procedure. In interviewing an accused, one must not depart from an assumption that the accused admitted to something that he did not admit to, nor can one put questions to him which already contain the answer the accused is supposed to give. That's deception in order to reach his statement or confession. This has been regulated in the criminal legislation of numerous European countries, and I would like, for instance, the law on the criminal procedure of Germany in division 10, Article 136(A), paragraph 2. And the law on criminal procedure of Austria, which is very precise in this regard. This is chapter 15, interrogation of the accused, Article 200, paragraph 2, which reads: "Questions attaching responsibility to the accused for the circumstances of the criminal offence which are only to be established in his answers and that contain easily recognisable suggestions that indicate his participation in the criminal offence which only has to be explored may be put to the accused only once the accused has accepted them. Otherwise, the evidence adduced in this manner shall be excluded." Your Honours shall keep in mind these facts whilst evaluating the probative value of the interview. It will keep in mind the fact that they used impermissible means in order to arrive at Oric's confession. They wished to accuse him at any cost. The longer you read the interview, the more convinced you will be that this is indeed the case. I will now take an example to illustrate the way the Prosecution has been using the interview and how in fact some sections of the interview were placed into the time context that assisted the Prosecution and which was incorrect, in order to show that Oric received reports, in other words, that he knew of crimes committed, and the way the interview is placed in the context of other evidence and what sort of evidence this is indeed. They are referring to P329, tape 8, page 10, paragraph 73 of the Prosecution reply to our final brief. Can we have slide number 10, please? Naser Oric: "The next attack was entrance into Glogova." Investigator: "So you're going to be speaking of Glogova now?" Oric: "Yes." "Which is between the Bjelovac attack and the next attack on Kravica. How many weeks passed between this attack and Kravica?" Naser Oric: "Between Glogova and Kravica?" Investigator: "Yes." Oric: "Let me tell you. First there was the entry, that's to say the Muslim village of Glogova." This was merely the introduction to show you the context which Oric is talking about. And then page 14 of the same part of the interview, in view of the fact that this action was not of a large scale, only people from TO Potocari took part in it and so only a team of Senad Golubovic who was commander of TO Pale went to Magasici. Senad Golubovic, yes, he went to Magasici. Your Honours, you will notice that Oric said "people from TO Potocari," and they interpreted it as "fighters from TO Potocari." For the Prosecution, it was crucial to confirm that the Pale company was part of the Potocari brigade at the time of the attack on Jezestica on the 8th of August, 1992, and at the time when, as they put it, Kemo killed and tortured prisoners. They are placing Kemo in the context of the events in the prison in the period between the 24th of September, 1992 and the 16th of October, 1992. According to the Prosecution, Kemo was a member of the Pale company, although their own witnesses testified otherwise. For instance, Dr. Mujkanovic. His testimony on the 14th of February, 2005, transcript pages 5041 to 5042; testimony on the 17th of February, 2005, transcript page 5253; and testimony on the 23rd of February, 2005, page 5440. Although they themselves used P590, whereby this same Kemo was in a completely different unit at the same time, and they wish to say that this confirm -- that Oric confirmed this in the mentioned part of the interview about Senad Golubovic. They wished to say that Oric had reports on the torching of houses and reported Kemo's criminal -- crimes. If you analyse the part of the interview they are referring to, you will find that Oric talks of events dating from late December 1992 concerning Glogova and Kravica. They are not talking about September/October 1992 or August 1992 as the Prosecution would wish you to believe and as the Prosecution seems to be using the interview for. There is no mention of the time frame in which the Prosecution wishes to place the subordination of the Pale company, Senad Golubovic and Kemo, to the Potocari Territorial Defence. In this context, Oric mentioned that Senad Golubovic had led the action on Magasici and that he was commander of the Pale TO. Therefore, he spoke of December 1992. Your Honours, Oric had repeatedly told the Prosecutor during the interview that his memory did not serve him well, and it is true that his memory didn't serve him well when he was giving the interview, because not even then, in December 1992, was Senad Golubovic able to be commander of the Pale TO for the simple reason that, according to the Prosecution, Exhibit P596, which the Prosecution also drew upon in order to demonstrate his subordination to Oric, because Senad Golubovic got killed on the 9th of October, 1992. You will see that on slide number 11 that Senad Golubovic got killed on the 9th of October, 1992, and here Oric spoke of him as being commander in December 1992. This is why Oric's memory is questionable, but also questionable are the intentions of the Prosecution in this case. They are simply stacking up evidence which one gets the impression they had never seemed to have analysed in the first place. The Prosecution is using them completely arbitrarily, regardless of the fact that the accuracy of that same evidence was called into question by their own witnesses. In their address on Monday, the Prosecution told us that the Defence witnesses simply refused to confirm the accuracy of their otherwise accurate evidence. Your Honours, I would like to break at this point by your leave because I am moving into a section where I would not like to have to stop.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see on the slide being a part of P80, and if you are to take a look at that -- at the text, this is the formation structure during the relevant period between the 17th of April, 1992 up until mid-October 1992. You will see that according to that document, Senad Golubovic was not the commander of the Pale company. It was Smajo Mandzic. This is at the bottom. In many parts of the Prosecutor's final brief, as well as in their reply to the Defence final brief and in their closing arguments, the Prosecution invoked the testimony of the accused. As to how it was procured you just saw a moment ago. It wasn't like the accused testified and under oath at that. Rather, he spoke with the representatives of the OTP as the Chamber itself put it yesterday. The probative value of the interview is something to be considered by the Chamber. In that consideration, you will have to bear in mind the fact that the law on criminal procedure of the former SFRY in its Article 218, as well as the law of the country of the accused, distinguish between examining an accused and testifying of a witness. According to those laws, the accused is not obliged to state his defence or to speak truthfully. According to the law, the accused is under -- is not under any obligation to speak the truth. That's why his statements -- statement cannot be given the same weight given to the Prosecutors. It was not given under oath and it cannot be ascribed, the same way ascribed to it by the Prosecutor. For all those reasons and the reasons I had already mentioned, this cannot be considered including the reasons stated in their application to exclude the interview with the accused. In their submissions, the Prosecutor stated that they do not believe certain portions of the interview but they do take them seriously when they seem fit. Such an example was the use of the book, "Srebrenica Testifies and Accuses," which was P90, used to prove that Oric knew of the attacks mentioned in the indictment. First of all, it is of no importance whether the accused knew whether such attacks occurred, but, rather, whether he knew that his subordinates committed crimes during those attacks. As to whether he had sufficient knowledge and information regarding that is what the true matter under consideration in this case is. In a part of his interview, on page 11 of tape 3 of P328, Oric clearly states that not only that he hadn't written the book but he didn't read it either. No witness confirmed the accuracy of many parts of that book that they were shown. The Prosecutor invoked other evidence as well to demonstrate that Oric knew of the crimes committed by his subordinates. In our reply to the Prosecutor's final brief, we wrote about the document P11 -- P111, allegedly demonstrating that the accused had specific information as to the torching, and this was in our reply in paragraphs 132, 133 and 134. In short, the Prosecutor created an elaborate construction to show that the accused indeed had knowledge of the torchings. Such construction is incorrect, and the document doesn't show anything stated by the Prosecutor. A few words about P161, they used for the same purpose. It is an unsigned document by an unknown author that hasn't been shown to any witness. Nothing on the face of the document shows that anyone at any time and anywhere received that document or that it had been sent to anyone. This is an alleged report to subregion commander dated the 29th of December, 1992, describing the attacks on Siljkovici, Banjavici and another four Serb villages. The document says that those villages were burned down but that Marici had not been torched completely. I will put this document in the context of the other Drina Corps documents pertaining to December 1992 and other Prosecution evidence portraying the situation in December of 1992, and the real situation in the aforementioned Serb villages. D18 [as interpreted], which is a document of the Bratunac Brigade command, dated the 3rd of December 1992, is a decision to attack, ordering the destruction of the Muslim villages. You can see a portion of that document before you. On page 3 of the document, in item 9, we see the description of -- Your Honours, I believe the number of the exhibit was recorded incorrectly. This was D819.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for this reason, it is very important that witnesses see the documents, especially those documents the authenticity of which is suspect for any reason. It is the standpoint of the OTP that our case as regards the documents is unfounded. The OTP states that our case that the witnesses had to see the documents is wrong. Moreover, in their closing arguments, they referred to the Appeals Chamber decision in the Blaskic case dated the 31st of October, 2003. In that decision, a certain Defence exhibits were accepted and, according to the Office of the Prosecutor, the Chamber referred in its decision to evidence not seen by any witness. Your Honours, their reasoning is completely incorrect. It is quite clear from the decision on evidence of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case of the 31st of December, 2003 that in that case the Defence was permitted to tender to the Appeals Chamber additional evidence not available to it during the trial. This was completely new evidence which the Defence was unable to come by previously. This also refers to Exhibit number 1 mentioned by Mr. di Fazio. This is natural, because this is new evidence, not available at the time of trial, and meeting the requirements of Rule 115. Therefore, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecutor is trying to compare what the Prosecution did in this case to what happened in the Blaskic case, where the Defence was permitted to use new evidence not available to it previously. Your Honour, there can be no comparison here. The Prosecutor sat on this evidence like a hen sitting on eggs, for years, while these proceedings continued. Numerous witnesses were heard, both Prosecution and Defence witnesses, who could have commented on these exhibits. The Defence checked. For each and every exhibit used here, they had it for years, and Your Honours can check this very easily, yet they did not show the exhibits to the witnesses. This was their tactical decision. They waited for the witnesses to turn their backs, and only then did they produce the documents. They wish to corroborate documents not seen or confirmed with other documents not seen or confirmed, and these with yet others, again not seen or confirmed. I'm sure that the Chamber will not allow this. Yesterday, the Prosecutor, in his closing arguments, showed the photograph of Philipp von Recklinghausen, P460, placing it in the context of Kravica, which was awash in blood and flame. They placed this photograph in the context of the 7th of January, 1993 in Kravica. Your Honours, you were able to see from the written statement of Mr. Recklinghausen that this photograph was taken in late February or early March 1993, as one of many photographs taken by him in the area. It does not depict any kind of celebration of success, as the Prosecutor wishes to imply, nor does it impress one as showing well-armed men. According to the Prosecutor's description of the equipment and weapons these people had, had one had one's eyes closed we would have imagined Naser sitting on a tank rather than a horse. The Prosecutor wishes to suggest that Oric could have seen the torched houses in Kravica. However, Your Honours, from the 7th of January, 1993, or early March 1993, when the events in Kravica alleged in the indictment took place, until the end of February or early March 1993, the Serb winter offensive was raging in the area. Kravica was bombed and shelled on a daily basis, including bombings from aircraft. Your Honours will recall the testimony of Sabra Kolenovic of the 31st of August, 2005, transcript pages 10112 to 10113. Your Honours, I wish to draw your attention to something I consider very important here. The submissions of the Prosecutor in this case are of such a nature that Your Honours will first of all have to deal not with legal issues raised by the Prosecutor, which is something only to be expected in a trial at an International Tribunal, but with the correctness of their allegations. You will need time to do this. Lacking evidence, they are simply inventing and fabricating evidence. In response to their submission, paragraphs -- in paragraphs 141 to 143, we showed how they invented that Akif Ustic spoke of torchings in Fakovici, whereas he mentioned the burning in the context of dugouts, and they invented the fact that the Muslims had two dugouts in the area. They knew that they had an incorrect translation or interpretation because they had received the correct one from the appropriate section of the Tribunal. They continued to claim that Zulfo Tursunovic talked of burnings in Bjelovac, although in that document it says that Zulfo said, Do not burn houses; P84.1, page 37 of the English version. Zulfo Tursunovic did not say anything else about burnings. Yesterday, speaking of the attitude to burnings in connection with the session of the 10th of January, 1993, page 49, Mrs. -- the Prosecutor, without batting an eyelid, said that it was only a staff session, not a joint session of the War Presidency and the staff, as if we would not check this. In fact, if you look at this session, you will see that it was attended by all the members, or almost all the members of the War Presidency, including Mr. Avdic personally, the president of the Presidency, and that Avdic was one of the people planning the action against Skelani. At that session, Ahmo said, burnings should not be allowed before the people from Skelani take their property back. However, if you look at page 50 of the English translation, you will see other conclusions there, one of which is, Naser's group is no longer to eat in the canteen; the next conclusion is food for the staff according to the decision of the War Presidency. This is the best indication of the kind of influence Naser Oric had among the members of the War Presidency. He could not even achieve that his people be allowed to eat in the kitchen or in the canteen. Based on these minutes of the 10th of January, 1993, one can see very well that Naser was not treated as a commander but as somebody who had a group of his own. Moreover, Naser was not even among the group of people planning the action or rather the attack on Skelani. In fact, Skelani was never set on fire. You will evaluate the professional conduct of the Prosecutor but we have our own opinion about it. Your Honours, I have just said that it is the Prosecution case that all the TO units in the Srebrenica area were under the effective control of the accused and that this case is highly disputed. In fact, the allegation made through the mouth of Hakija Meholjic, what actually transpired was that the accused only had control over a small group of his fighters in Potocari, Naser's men. That is what is evident from the document I have just mentioned. He was not in control of the other groups who elected their own leaders and acted on a voluntary basis. If they wanted to, they participated in an action, but if they didn't want to, they didn't. In our closing brief, we speak in detail of the improvised, voluntary, local nature of the fighting in Srebrenica, and I will not repeat our submissions here. I will now speak of the meeting in Bajramovici. I will not repeat once more, Your Honours, what we have stated in our written submissions about the meeting in Bajramovici in our final brief and in our response to the Prosecution brief, but I will say the following. The Prosecution has given this meeting a significance it does not have. The reality was much more mundane. The group leaders, quite understandably, addressed each other, saying, "Let's see whether we can help each other in our common fight against the Serbs." Do documents P73 and P75 reflect with precision the decisions that were made is a question we cannot go into here today, but we have done this in our final brief. Your Honours, even were these exhibits authentic, they do not reflect anything further than an intention to establish a staff. An intention is one thing, whereas the implementation of the intention is something quite different. According to the Prosecution, the act of putting pencil to paper is a mystical event which transforms everything that is written into reality in the actual world. According to the Prosecution, events can become real by typing or by writing. It was sufficient to write down the words "unified command," and a unified command would be established that very moment. Of course, the reality was quite different. It is not hard to imagine people under siege, people who are trapped, who have already lost many friends and family members, who have seen the Serbs set fire to Srebrenica, elderly people being burnt alive in their homes, people trying to strengthen themselves and their decisiveness by announcing a grand plan to establish a TO staff or by celebrating the anniversary of that staff. However, did it really function? You cannot get the answer to that from a piece of paper or from the video shown on Monday, P433, on which you saw Naser reading out a prepared speech intended to encourage the people and give them hope, to convince the people that there is someone looking after them and that they have something in common. Did the unified command actually function in practice? Only witnesses can give you the answer to that. And they have given the answer. They said decisively that the unified command never actually came to life. All the Defence witnesses and all the Prosecution witnesses who testified about the situation in Srebrenica, Hakija Meholjic, Ibrahim Becirovic, Omer Ramic, Hamed Tiro, Nesib Buric, Azir Malagic, Ibro Alic, Ejub Dedic, D005, Suad Smajlovic, and others. Prosecution witness General Sead Delic, commenting on P129, and this is a document containing an order to mobilise the municipal TO Srebrenica staff within 12 hours, dated September 1992 said on the 30th of May, 2005, on transcript pages 8693 and 8695: "My comment is a piece of paper can withstand anything. It can take anything." And he explained. "This is a phrase we use in the Bosnian language, which means that you can write whatever you like on a piece of paper. However, when it has to be implemented that's where the problems arise." The Prosecution case that the meeting in Bajramovici resulted in the establishment of a unified command is just theory. It has not been confirmed by witnesses but, on the contrary, it has been disputed by witnesses more than once, and this includes Prosecution witnesses. Not only this. Numerous towns and villages did not participate in the meeting in Bajramovici, nor did they know about it or about any decisions made there. These decisions were not binding upon them. To start with, not a single town or village in which the Muslims retained control in Bratunac, Zvornik or Vlasenica municipalities, participated in that. These were simply different municipalities. In these municipalities, they also had their groups. They organised their own War Presidencies. They organised their own staffs of Territorial Defence. Please bear in mind, Your Honours, that only one out of five attacks alleged in the indictment was conducted in the Srebrenica area, and this one was in the Ratkovici area. The others were not. The evidence has shown that the groups from Bratunac, Vlasenica and Zvornik took part in all these events. You should recall the Bratunac groups. These are Ejub Golic's group, Nurif Rizvanovic's group with the 400 men from Tuzla at Konjevic Polje, the group from Jagodnja and Joseva, Zanjevo, Abdulici, Voljavica. Many groups of Konjevic Polje that were testified about in this case. Remember the groups from Vlasenica, the group of Becir Mekanic, the group from Cerska that Mr. Dedic testified about. Remember Muhamed Sekiric and the Zvornik groups, which Mr. Dedic also testified about. All of these groups, up until the time when these areas fell, that's to say up until demilitarisation, operated outside Srebrenica. It wasn't Sefer Halilovic in document P76, or President Izetbegovic in P33 who placed under Oric's jurisdiction or command, whichever way you take it, the units from the municipalities of Bratunac, Vlasenica and Zvornik. If these documents had ever reached Srebrenica, which has not been proved by the Prosecutor beyond a reasonable doubt, then they must have had to do only with the municipalities of Srebrenica and its Territorial Defence. The Prosecutor said that it was only Oric's name that was mentioned in the context of Srebrenica. This does not -- does say -- it says about the lack of information about -- among the people who came to Srebrenica, about what was happening in Srebrenica, and that there were no people in Srebrenica who were able to do the jobs that they were supposed to do. Therefore, the Prosecutor asserts, and it is completely unfounded, that, according to P33, Oric was authorised to issue orders to Ejub Golic because this wasn't the case. Glogova is part of Bratunac municipality. In Srebrenica municipality, only six places or villages took part at the Bajramovici meeting. According to Prosecution Exhibit P73, these were Potocari, Srebrenica, Suceska, Bajramovici, Bojna and possibly Skelani, although not likely, because Skelani was held by Serbs. Osmace, Kragljivoda and Skenderovici were added to this staff on the 26th of May, 1992, according to Exhibit P75. Your Honour, on Monday, the Prosecution quoted Bogilovic's words, according to which the decision taken at Bajramovici was binding on the groups that met there. These were nine locations out of dozens of villages in Srebrenica, which had their own independent armed groups, which fought the local Serbs, all of which took part in the events alleged in the indictment. In our final brief, we mentioned more than 20 such locations. How can someone say that it can be established beyond reasonable doubt that the fighters of these groups did not wantonly destroy property in any action but that the fighters from the groups which took part at the Bajramovici meeting did? Lastly, how can the Prosecution continue asserting that the accused had effective control over the groups that met at Bajramovici when their own evidence says that Ustic and Tursunovic among others were not under the accused's control? Testifying to that effect were Hakija Meholjic on the 8th of April, 2005, transcript page 6948; on the 6th of April, 2005, transcript page 6810; Becir Bogilovic, their own witness, 22nd of March, 2005, transcript page 6419; Ibrahim Becirovic, also a Prosecution witness, on the 25th of April, 2005, transcript pages 7625 and 7631. The Bajramovici meeting was merely an attempt on the part of courageous individuals to coordinate their efforts in their fight against Serbs. For the Prosecution, this meant a second Yalta. From the closing arguments of the Prosecution, it clearly transpires that the Prosecution wishes to paint the picture of a level of organisation of Srebrenica fighters that grew increasingly better over time in 1992. At the same time, they wish to prove the strengthening of the power of the accused because a document was drafted expanding his powers. Your Honours, the reality was quite different. I will mention only some of the factors which had a bearing on the reality and defined it as it was. Our Exhibit, D75, showed the order of the General Staff the army of the Republika Srpska to destroy Ustasha forces in the region of Birac, ordering an offensive. The report of the command of the Drina Corps dated 4 November 1992, Defence Exhibit D921 [as interpreted], demonstrated that. I quote: "After several months of fighting in the areas of Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, the combat operations have reached their final stage. The enemy has been pushed back into a very small area at the centre of which is Konjevic Polje. They are encircled and on the verge of a full military defeat." The commander of the Drina Corps, Milenko Zivanovic, held a speech on the occasion of the establishment of the Bratunac Brigade on the 14th of November, 1992, and announces: "I expect the winter to be our ally because the results of the fighting to date are striking and grand. How grand? Well, we are holding 80.000 Turks in encirclement. The Turks from Cerska can't stand the sight of the Turks from Srebrenica. Those from Kladanj don't go along with those from Srebrenica or from Cerska. Those from Zepa can't go to Srebrenica. Those in Gorazde can't go to Zepa. These are really grand results when regarded from a broader perspective." And these are words of the commander of the Drina Corps. Your Honour, I will repeat a section of what I said because it was not correctly reflected. And I quote what Colonel Zivanovic said: "Well, we are holding 80.000 Turks in encirclement. Turks from Cerska can't see those Turks from Srebrenica. Kladanjski can't even with those from Srebrenica or from Cerska. Those from Zepa can't go to Srebrenica and those from Gorazde can't go to Zepa. These are really grand results when regarded from a broader perspective." In commenting this speech by the commander of the Drina Corps, the Prosecution witness, Dr. James Gow, stated on the 23rd of November, 2004, at page 1924 [as interpreted], the following: "It is consistent with many other matters I've already said. This indicates that there was an approach which meant isolating and surrounding places, cutting them off and eventually entering them in order to cleanse them when there is a chance to do that." On the 19th of November, 1992, the General Staff of the VRS issued a new directive to the effect that the enemy be tired in the general area of Podrinje and that it be compelled to leave the areas of Birac with the Muslim population. This is our D76. This order was forwarded by the command of the Drina Corps to the commands of the subordinate units on the 24th of November, 1992 with the following task, among others: "That the Muslim population be forced to leave the areas of Zepa, Cerska and Gorazde and that the enemy forces be routed and pushed out." That's our D928. In our final brief, in the part which has to do with attacks, we presented a number of documents which point to numerous attacks and the cutting off of Cerska and Konjevic Polje which, Your Honour, ought to be parts of the subregion. It was precisely to these areas that Oric's reportedly expanded powers applied, these areas that were cut off. About the actual situation in these areas, in the course of the autumn and summer months of -- or in the winter months of 1992, the following witnesses testified: Izet Redzic, Ejub Dedic, D005, Ejub Guster and many others. The idea that this subregion was able to function constitutes the other part of the Prosecution case. Not a single witness confirmed that the subregion functioned. Quite the contrary. Both Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses testified that the subregion had never functioned because of the winter offensive of the Serbs, the humanitarian catastrophe in Srebrenica, and the general chaos that reigned there in this period of time. The Prosecution wishes to persuade you that several written orders, mostly those by Hamed Salihovic, are proof of the fact that the subregion functioned because the documents exist, regardless of what even the Prosecution witnesses had to say about this. The best illustration of what is stated in the documents on the one hand, and what the actual reality was, on the other, is the testimony given on the 14th of December, 2005, transcript page 15032, by Witness Lieutenant-Colonel Rex Dudley whilst commenting Prosecution documents. I'm quoting: "In view of what I saw, there was a large difference between intentions and possibilities. This document indicates an intention. Whatever the case, I doubt that the forces on the ground had had the possibility to effectively execute this order." Prosecution witnesses stated that in the course of the winter in 1992 and 1993, the situation in the Srebrenica area became disastrous. Colonel Tucker, who they referred to so many times these past days, described how the Serbian pacmen steadily engulfed village by village in early 1993 in applying the strategy of merciless terrorism by artillery, as he put it, which was then normally followed by infantry attacks. Your Honours, in wartime, just as in life in general, matters don't always take the best course. In this case, the situation in Srebrenica did not improve, nor were they able to improve their organisation. The events that unfolded in the months prior to the demilitarisation led to a catastrophe. Things went from bad to worse. And only the proclamation of a protected zone saved people from massacre in April 1993. Even the Prosecution witnesses stated that what happened in July 1995, that terrible tragedy, was merely a continuation of events from 1992 and 1993. Had Serbs seized the town back then, it could easily have happened two or three years earlier. Despite all these facts, the Prosecution continues to believe in their disproved case that until the end of 1992 the accused was at the head of this large subregion constituted by the municipalities of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Srebrenica and Zvornik. Moreover, in Annex D of their final trial brief, the Prosecution is attempting to show the boundaries of this subregion. Can we please see slide number 14? Your Honours, please take a look at what the boundaries of the subregion ought to be. According to the Prosecution map, which they present in Annex D of their final trial brief, please take a look, the towns of Vlasenica and Milici were under Muslim control -- of the Muslim forces, including Naser Oric. Just as the towns of Bratunac and Zvornik. Take a look at the map, please. In fact, all these towns were held by Serbs, already back in April 1992, up until the end of the war. The truth and reality are things and matters quite different, quite something different. The Muslims actually controlled small parts -- and you will recall that thousands of Muslims were killed in these areas that they never mentioned. What is the truth is that Muslims controlled only small parts of the municipalities, parts of Bratunac, in the area of Konjevic Polje, Glogova mount, and Bljeceva, parts of Vlasenica, the area of Cerska, a small part in the Zvornik municipality in the area of Kamenica, and not even all the parts of Srebrenica municipality. Naturally, the people in the areas wanted to get united. Of course, they attempted to do so. You heard, and numerous witnesses confirmed that, that Hamed Salihovic did whatever he could. He wrote orders and, as witnesses confirmed, that's where it all stopped. There Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was nothing to follow up on these orders. Your Honours, I will now move on to the topic of the ability of the accused to control the enclave. You have our submissions, and this particular position is stated in paragraph 12 [as interpreted] of the final defence brief. Still, I wanted to mention this briefly today. The extent of desperation amongst the members of the enclave by the end of December 1992 is best illustrated by their own enemy's document; that is, the army of Republika Srpska from the Bratunac Brigade command dated the 28th of December, 1992, which is D807. This is a report in which the Serb military command describes the behaviour of Muslim civilians on their way to Glogova. It states --
