utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Chapter, part 12, starting at page 1413. Sorry for having interrupted you, Ms. Vidovic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your intervention, Your Honour. I started quoting the Bratunac Brigade command report, D807. In this report, that particular Serb military command describes the behaviour of Muslim civilians on their way to Glogova. They were trying to go back to the place where they were expelled from in May 1992. I quote a part of that document: "According to your assessment, in that region there are around 500 fighters and a far greater number of civilians, women and children. That is around 1.000 of them. Their numbers increase in evening hours. They move freely in columns, in spite of constant artillery fire." Your Honours, this is a document describing people moving freely in columns although they were fired upon from artillery. This is mind-boggling. The Prosecutor imagines that such desperation could be controlled. They had no fear of death. They moved under artillery fire and, on occasion, listening to the witnesses we had, it sounded impossible, but this is clearly portrayed by the Bratunac Brigade report. In order for you to assess the possibility of control, you can make use of an exhibit put forth by the Prosecutor. It was Hakija Meholjic in his testimony of the 8th of April, 2005, page 6961 of the transcript, and he mentioned what the circumstances and conditions should be for a commander to exercise effective control over his subordinates. He said the following on slide 15: "There was nothing in place to provide for an efficient control. Not even the organised military of the United States cannot control all of its troops, let alone us. We were not organised. Secondly, there were no corps. There was no mechanism to punish a soldier. You could only beat him or chase him out of your ranks. There were no institutions as such in place." Prosecution theory relies on the idea that the accused was some sort of king in the enclave. In their pre-trial brief, they described him as follows: Naser Oric was the highest authority in the enclave, loved by the people of the area as if he were a king. They clung to the theory of Naser as king throughout. But still, when it was put to Dr. Mujkanovic, who supposedly had to corroborate that, he said the following. Can we have slide number 16, please? Question put to Dr. Mujkanovic: "When the Prosecution opened the case against Naser Oric last October, Mr. Wubben said that Naser Oric was a war lord, drunk with power. Is that how Naser Oric struck you? "Answer: No. Certainly not. Drunk with power? There was no power to speak of in Srebrenica. What sort of power? To be anything in Srebrenica, where you could hardly survive, it was a punishment rather than power." One needs to read these lines carefully: What sort of power? To be anything in Srebrenica where you could hardly survive. There was no power to be had in Srebrenica at that time. One only be a sitting duck waiting for its turn to be killed. The accused, as a war lord, displaying his drunkenness with power is yet another cliche, a myth put forth by Prosecution with their evidence. Still, Dr. Mujkanovic described that the accused praised the virtues of other fighters and never spoke about himself. He was very young and he carried a great burden. It was one of Prosecution's witnesses, Colonel Tucker, was far more realistic and humane in his opinion of the accused than Prosecution had ever been. He said: "He worked in the most hostile and difficult circumstances. I can even picture myself working under such circumstances. One couldn't speak of any power, and in particular about that sort of power needed to control thousands of desperate and malnourished civilians." This is important to be put in the context, not as background noise but as one of life's realities. There were refugees, unknown, unidentified, unregistered. They flooded Srebrenica in masses during the time, because of the ethnic cleansing conducted by the Serbs in local villages. How could anyone control such miserable masses? The context is of crucial importance, in order to assess that. There was no functioning military police, the judiciary or prosecutors; there were no rules or regulations that people in Srebrenica could rely on to organise their life in the enclave, as testified by Judge Mesud Omerovic on the 26th of May, 2005, and this was at another Prosecution witness, when he commented the situation in late 1992 and early 1993. Could we please see slide number 17? I quote: "Every day it was said that Srebrenica was to fall. I didn't address anybody about their lack of work in the period from October 1992 to May 1993. It was on account of the terrible humanitarian situation and that nothing was working in Srebrenica. The surrounding villages were falling under Serb control one after the other. The refugees had filled the whole of Srebrenica. The working of the court was not a priority at that time. The town was dying, and it was not possible to pay attention to such things." Your Honours, it wasn't only Bosniak Mesud Omerovic who saw the situation as such. It was seen the same way by the international witnesses who were in Srebrenica at the time, Dr. Dachy, in his testimony on a report by an international organisation on the situation in the enclave, being D711, dated the 11th of July, 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The testimony was on the 11th of July, 2005, page 9460 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Confirmed the truthfulness of the image portrayed by the report on Srebrenica. I quote: "The population of Srebrenica had been completely isolated from the outside world, made to cope any which way it could. Sometimes it is impossible to put coping mechanisms in place in the short period or even in the long run for as long as the Bosnian Serbs were in their positions. There were no water sources, no sources of energy supply, no institutions, no people, and no means to put such institutions in place." Further down the report states: "They were all facing the same problems. They had no qualified staff to run these institutions and they were not to come from Sarajevo or Tuzla. The idea of an enclave looking after itself as best it can surrounded by an enemy population is a complete illusion." Your Honours, I quoted a document by an important international organisation. The fact that Srebrenica at the time looked like the Lord of the Flies by William Golding, is not sheer background, just another fact that can be recorded and then ignored. All of the facts in this case are closely linked to reality. And the reality shows the following facts. There were no institutions or they were not functional. The Prosecutor would have you convinced that this was not so, although their own witnesses stated that. They put forth entire theories of military police. They claimed that the military police was functional and equipped. Yesterday they stated that it was Defence who would suggest to you that the military police was unequipped and that they had only two guns, two rifles. To remind the Prosecutor, it wasn't said by Defence but, inter alia, it was stated in their own exhibit they used extensively. That was P84. Your Honours, I wanted to quote the last sentence on page 34 of the English of this document, P84, pertaining to a meeting of the armed forces staff of Srebrenica dated the 4th of December, 1992. The 4th of December. Krdzic, Atif, states: "The military police had not been completed. Many gave up because of food and accommodation. There are no weapons, only two guns and two rifles." Therefore, this wasn't put forth by Defence but, rather, by their own favourite document, P84. The role of the military police in the conditions of war in Srebrenica was not as the Prosecutor imagines it was. It couldn't have been, because there were no regulations, no military organisation, or military rules in place. The Prosecutor was trying to prove that the staff headed by Oric appointed Atif Krdzic as military police commander. They claim that he was subordinated to the staff. In order to show that, they used patrol orders, alleged patrol orders by the military police, P15, 16 and 17, as well as documents P11 and P12. They used P561, that is P458, and again they used the war diary, P84. To stress yet again, the Prosecutor used exhibits, the validity of which was not confirmed by anyone. Nobody confirmed the contents of these documents. Quite the contrary. The validity of the contents of the patrol orders, P15, 16 and 17, was denied by their own witnesses, C007 and Ms. Andza Radovic [phoen]. The Prosecutor interviewed Dzanan Dzananovic, the military policeman whose name appears in those orders. His statement is our D139. He himself put those documents in question. He told the Prosecutor that he had never seen the documents and that the signature on P17 and P333 is not his. He wasn't called to testify, as were not many other witnesses who expressed their doubts as to the authenticity of their documents. Some of them even clearly stated that those documents were fabricated and that they had nothing to do with them. I will go back to P17. They didn't call Dzanan Dzananovic to testify, but they sent the document for handwriting examination. Their expert concluded that the signature on document P17 probably is not that of Dzananovic. Rather, he ruled out the possibility that it was Dzananovic's signature. It was the same type of patrol order as P15 and P16. Your Honours, is that a part of that theory, conspiracy theory, as Mr. di Fazio said yesterday? Unbelievably still, the Prosecutor relies on these documents to confirm that Krdzic was appointed by the staff and that he was under its control, irrespective of the fact that there is sufficient evidence not to use those documents. They use P84 to try and corroborate it, claiming that at the meeting of the 22nd of November, 1992, Krdzic was appointed military police commander by the staff, and that the War Presidency was not present. First of all, that is not correct. The Prosecutor never invested an effort in order to understand who the people at those meetings were, what their names were, and what their so-called functions or titles in Srebrenica were. Had they done that, they would have known that Suljo Hasanovic, who on page 02115072, page 22 in the English, of the same document, is mentioned as a member of the Executive Board of the War Presidency for All People's Defence, and on page 02115051, page 8 of the English, as the person in the War Presidency tasked with All People's Defence. There was no Suljo within the staff, and at the meeting of the 22nd of November, 1992, Suljo was there, seconding the comments made by some other people. Your Honours, it seems that the Prosecutor and their policy is to remain silent on such parts of documents they don't like and to interpret it the way they seem fit. Could we please see slide number 18? It's also part of P84, and I will quote from it: "Osman reported on the position of the RP regarding the reorganisation of the VP. A request for the dismissal of the commander was also read. Hamed, there have been failures. In the town there should be a VP squad attached to the staff." Your Honours, the date of what you see here is the 22nd of November, 1992. When you take a look at what was actually discussed on -- at the session of the 22nd of November, 1992, you will see that Osman Osmanovic reported about the standpoint of the War Presidency on the reorganisation of the military police. Therefore, what was discussed at the meeting was the standpoint of the War Presidency on the reorganisation of the military police. It was in this context that Mirzet Halilovic was mentioned. It says here that a request was read out to dismiss the commander, as well as Atif Krdzic. It's quite clear from this part of the document which they refer that in the town, a VP squad is needed in the town, which means at the very least that at that point in time there was no military police squad attached to the staff; otherwise, why would they be requesting one? They referred to P561 or P458, claiming that the military police was not subordinate to the War Presidency. P561, let me remind you, is a document which was allegedly found on a field. Unlike those who call it the diary of the military police, we call it the field diary. And that's a diary in which it says, under the date the 6th of December, 1992, I quote: "I was walking along the street while the bus was leaving the bus station to go to Bratunac." As you know, Your Honours, there were no buses in Srebrenica in December 1992 and especially there was no traffic through the firing lines. This document cannot be correct. Take another look, Your Honours, as the Prosecution documents which they rely on in an attempt to prove that the military police was subordinate to the staff. Both of the documents you will see now have been used by the Prosecutor in the same paragraph, 44, of their response to our final brief. They use both documents in an attempt to corroborate the allegation that it was the staff that issued orders to the military police. Please take a look at the document on slide 19. It's document P15, Your Honours, which I have just mentioned. It says: "Patrols in town," and Mr. Atif is mentioned as the commander of the military police, Atif Krdzic. And you will see that it says on the seal, Srebrenica, Potocari, which doesn't have much to do with the military police. And then please pay attention to the second part of the document, which says: "Report of the patrols in town, dated the 9th of January, 1993, time 0600 to 1400 hours." And it says: "At 1200 hours, acting on the same Srebrenica OS staff order we sealed up two blacksmith shops and took the keys to the police. At 1300 hours, we took two prisoners of war to the OS staff for interviewing." Now, please let us see slide 20. Your Honours, this is now part of document P561 through 458 dated the 13th of January, 1993, and it says: "On the orders of Suljo Hasanovic, who had a written receipt, I opened the blacksmith's shop to Idriz Mehic and handed him the keys. The aforementioned blacksmiths was shut down, (sealed) on the 9th of January, 1993 at the order of the Secretariat for National Defence." Your Honours, once again, this is the kind of evidence the Prosecution has produced. It always -- there are always discrepancies. However, they wish you not to believe those parts of the documents that do not fit their case. Which of these two documents should you believe, Your Honours? Because, according to their two documents, which fortunately for us, deal with exactly the same event of the 9th of January, 1993, the blacksmith shop, and we see that the order to the military police in connection with the blacksmith shops was issued by two different bodies. According to P15 by the staff, and according to P561 and P458, the Secretariat for National Defence. You will recall that will this was part of the War Presidency of Srebrenica. The Prosecutor wants to say that both are correct when they deal with the issuing of orders to the military police. According to their Exhibit P561, P458, on the 10th of December, 1992, five men from the military police are put at the disposal of the staff. Why would those people from the military police be put at the disposal of the staff on that date if the military police, as the Prosecution alleges, was subordinate to the staff? There is no logic there. Your Honours, this might be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, because before the break I was in the middle of making -- taking a note. Yes. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In their response to our brief, our final brief, in paragraph 45, the Prosecutor alleges that there is no evidence in their document P561 that the military police received orders from the War Presidency. However, this is not the case. You will remember the testimony of Mrs. Suhra Djilovic, the administrative secretary of the War Presidency, of the 17th of January on -- of 2005 [as interpreted], on page 15235, who stated clearly that the War Presidency was attempting to get firewood for the hospital by organising farmers to transport the firewood on horses. You have the slide here, Your Honours, and you will see the entry of the 8th of December, 1992, referring to a session of the War Presidency at which there is discussion of something falling within the purview of the military police and allegedly signed by the author of this diary who is purportedly a military policeman. You will see that they discuss a curfew and an agreement to stop daily shooting incidents in the town. Please show the next slide. Your Honours, this is part of -- the part of the document that follows the previous one. It's the very next page. And I wanted to show it to you because, according to the Prosecutor, as stated in paragraph 45 of their response, this page is supposed to be an order issued by Naser Oric. However, from what you see on the slide, you will see that it is a draft of a patrol order, as envisaged by someone. The Prosecutor alleges in paragraph 45 of their response to our final brief that this is an order issued by Naser Oric. However, this piece of paper has nothing whatsoever to do either with any kind of order or with Naser Oric. Please show the next slide now. I am going through the diary in sequence. Immediately after this alleged patrol order, allegedly issued by Naser Oric, is an entry referring to the 10th of December, 1992, referring to -- calls upon owners of pack animals to bring firewood for the hospital. This was the task of the War Presidency in Srebrenica, and you will recall that Mrs. Djilovic talked in detail about how the War Presidency found firewood and procured firewood for the hospital in Srebrenica. By no means does this document show what the Prosecutor wants it to show, that is that the military police did not carry out orders issued by the War Presidency. In our final brief, we gave other examples showing that the War Presidency did, in fact, issue orders to the military police. This is described in our paragraph 628 to 646. The Prosecutor attaches great significance to the fact that in some places in P561, the commander of the military police is addressed as the commander of the military police of the armed forces of Srebrenica. Your Honours, in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the former Yugoslavia in general, the term "armed forces" had a far wider meaning than the one attached to it by the Prosecutor. In the general confusion in Srebrenica, the lack and the ignorance of regulations and legislation and adequate terminology, something that is written down does not necessarily reflect the actual situation. That is why Your Honours heard witnesses and what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses said about the appointment and control of Atif Krdzic. Suhra Djilovic, the administrative secretary of the War Presidency of Srebrenica testifying on the 17th of January, 2005, on page 15235 said as follows: "Yes, I remember Atif Krdzic was appointed after Mirzet Halilovic. "Question: Do you remember who appointed Atif Krdzic? "Answer: Yes. The War Presidency." A little further on there was a question as follows: "According to what you know, to whom was Krdzic subordinated? "Answer: To Becir Bogilovic, the chief." On the 13th [as interpreted] of October, 2005, on pages 13287 to 13288 of the transcript, this testimony was corroborated by Mustafa Sacirovic who, like Mrs. Djilovic, was in the situation to know what went on in the War Presidency because he worked there, as did Mrs. Djilovic. The Prosecutor did not, pursuant to Rule 90(H)(ii) put to these witnesses the nature of his case, which is contrary to their testimony. Certainly, it was the sacred and solemn duty of Prosecution counsel to put their case in cross-examination. We always did so. You will find in many places in the submissions by the Prosecutor that Prosecution witnesses categorically rejected some things put to them by the Defence. Whether Your Honours will believe that rejection or not is a different matter. But we as Defence counsel made it possible for Prosecution witnesses to respond to our suggestions whenever there was an issue we did not agree on. Why am I saying this now? Because it is impermissible that months after the witnesses have left, the Prosecutor finds questions where they -- and issues in which they disagree with Defence witnesses without ever having put their case to those witnesses. And not only this, they heard the same kind of testimony from their own witnesses, and they did not even try to impeach these witnesses. This was the case, for example, with the documents which I say they had for years but they did not put these documents even to their own witnesses. This was the case, inter alia, with Prosecution witness Hakija Meholjic and his statement that the military police, from its very founding in early July 1992, was within the structure of the civilian police. Hakija Meholjic, who was appointed chief of the Public Security Service in Srebrenica in April 1993, and in that capacity certainly knew about the situation and the relations that he found in the military police on the 8th of April, 2005 testified on pages 6992 to 6993 that he found the military police and Atif Krdzic within the structure of the civilian police, that he had certain complications and problems with Krdzic, but that he managed to solve those. When asked the following: "Mr. Meholjic, you said clearly that before your appointment, the military police was part of the civilian police within the structure of the civilian police." The answer was: "Yes. There is no dispute about that. I have repeated that more than once." Let us see what another Prosecution witness had to say about the military police, namely Judge Mesud Omerovic. In his testimony on the 25th [as interpreted] of May, 2005, page 8537, he described the military police as follows -- Your Honours, there is slide number 24 for you to see there. "Its composition, level of equipment, necessary knowledge, education level of the staff, did not allow them to run a procedure or to submit a report. I do not think they did anything regarding public security. That job was done by the civilian police." He confirmed that in Srebrenica, at the time, it was believed that the task of the civilian police was that of initiating proceedings against perpetrators of misdemeanours and criminal offences and any other duties in the realm of public security. Could we have slide number 25 now, please? Throughout the trial, the Prosecution has been trying to persuade you that the authority over the military police, prison, prisoners and exchanges was held by the staff. That's to say by Naser Oric. Look at document P45. This is their exhibit, a document by the municipality of Srebrenica, War Presidency of Srebrenica, dated 9 February 1993. If this is an authentic document, then it states that the War Presidency was the one dealing with prisoners and their exchanges. In this case, the document confirms this beyond any doubt. This is a document of the War Presidency, bearing the stamp of the War Presidency and the type of signature we were able to see in other documents as Avdic's signature. In this case, this very Prosecution evidence confirms everything the witnesses Suhra Djilovic and Mustafa Sacirovic said, including documents D987 and D866, the so-called Karno video clip and Karno document, which showed the communication concerning prisoners between Mr. Jusufovic, commander of the civilian police, and Mr. Avdic. This particular piece of evidence relating to the military police, prison and prisoners was adduced by the Prosecution themselves. Now they are claiming something quite different. The Prosecution asserts that a military court was established in Srebrenica and that Oric had the legal basis for setting up a special military court. In actual fact, their own witness, Prosecution Witness Enver Hodzic, in his testimony on the 11 May 2005, pages 8073 and 8074, he stated: "In the time period between 1992 and 1995, or 1996, for as long as I was a member of the army, this type of court had never been set up in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps." He is therefore mentioning the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, and that's a Prosecution witness speaking, which include -- the area of responsibility which includes Srebrenica. This -- it is quite cynical that the Prosecutor should be referring to the regulations of the newly established state of the BiH when at least five of their own witnesses, namely Brkic, Hogic, Omerovic, Meholjic and Becirovic stated that the regulations were never either sent or received, sent to or received in Srebrenica. That the military court was set up in Srebrenica is confirmed by the Prosecutor through the war diary, P84, because that is what the war diary says. Regardless of the fact that their witness, Judge Omerovic, who attended precisely the meeting they are referring to, held on the 9th of November, 1992, stated in his testimony on the 25th of May, 2005, on page 8456, and I'm literally quoting: "It says military court here but I can claim with full responsibility that a decision setting up the court was not passed at this meeting, nor was it put to a vote. Actually, I'm absolutely certain that this is a mistaken interpretation of the person that kept the minutes." Your Honours, this fact is quite telling in terms of weight you can attach to Prosecution Exhibit P84. Yesterday, the Prosecutor said something that was not correct in connection with P84. The Defence has never accepted either the authenticity or the accuracy of the document because it is aware of the background of the document. Your Honour, yesterday, in order to attach greater weight and seriousness to the document, they stated that the document was officially certified and registered in special official files. Can we please take a look at slide number 27? Your Honours, please take a look at the slide. It says here that the document was certified and that it has 100 sheets of paper. Of course, admittedly, in English, it was translated as 100 pages. You will recall, Your Honours, that at the start of trial, we submitted that, on the face of it, one could see that there were pages missing. Moreover, we stated right at the start that the diary was written in two different handwritings. If indeed it is true that the diary was certified as argued by the Prosecution, then it is true that at the moment of its certification, it had 100 sheets of paper, not pages. Your Honours reviewed the document and the Defence team inspected the document twice. Whichever way you count the pages of the diary, you will see that it has either 67 sheets of paper. In our language, we call a piece of paper that was written on on both sides a sheet of paper. Therefore, it has either 67 sheets of paper or 134 pages. We established this by carefully inspecting the diary and you yourselves noticed that at the very start of the trial. At any rate, we are not dealing with 100 pages. In the course of testimony of expert witness de Koeijer, Your Honours themselves noticed that there were pages missing. I'm referring to his testimony on the 13th of October, 2004, pages 652 to 655, and we presented the expert witness with different handwritings. His answer was: "The Prosecution did not request that I examine the handwriting and I did not do it." That's transcript page 681 of the testimony on the 13th of October, 2004. Your Honours, we are submitting accordingly that P84 should not be accorded the weight the OTP attaches to it. Yesterday, the Prosecution showed you one clip of the interview which again is going to be very telling about the Prosecution approach to this case. I'm speaking of the following part of the interview, P328, tape 13, pages 7 and 8 of the English version. Your Honours, I do not have the time to play that part to you again, but you will remember that in this part Oric stated that during a break at the time he took part in the interview, he learned from some fighters that the military court was set up after the action at Zalazje and that later on Zulfo Tursunovic was, as he put it, some sort of military judge at the military court. This in fact tells you how Oric obtained information for the interview, although I mentioned it for a completely different reason. In this part of the interview he goes on to say: "The reason we appointed him was that he was a man who had spent many years in prison." He then goes on to explain quite clearly that Zulfo was in prison because he had himself committed a criminal offence and convicted to a sentence of several years. The Prosecution presented this part to you yesterday as if Oric said that Zulfo had spent a lot of time in prison because he was working in the prison during the war and that therefore Oric was able to receive information about prisoners from him. Such distortion of facts is rarely to be seen in case law, Your Honours. We trust the Trial Chamber and we believe that something of the sort will not mislead them. The Prosecution argues that Oric had the possibility to communicate with subordinates and superiors. What's more, the Prosecution states that the possibility of communicating with the subordinates and superiors is one element of the reasonable measures for exercising effective control by a commander. Therefore, they state that Oric had reasonable means of communication to exercise effective control over their subordinates. To corroborate this, the Prosecution stated that the Muslim forces had led very successful military actions from June 1992 up until March 1993. Your Honours, first of all, it is completely incorrect that the Muslim forces conducted any sort of action, let alone a successful one, after the 16th of January, 1993. There are numerous documents of the Drina Corps demonstrating this. As for those successful actions, I'd rather call them struggles by desperate people for bare survival. In paragraph 644 of their final trial brief, the Prosecution mocked the fact that these successful actions were achieved even at the cost of dozens of dead who had to tread through minefields. The Prosecution should be ashamed of such reasoning. They should be ashamed of these words put on paper, because they will be read by people who are survivors. As the Honourable Chamber knows, in Srebrenica, people died of hunger. They were shocked by shelling and desperate. People can make incredible achievements in despair. In one of the Nazi concentration camps, a group of prisoners who were sent to gas chambers managed to break through a brick wall in a frenetic attempt to avoid death. This would not be convincing, according to our Prosecution. In the Warsaw ghetto the barely armed members of the Jewish resistance movement stood ground to the enormous German army for 28 days. Our Prosecution would complacently write, "This is unbelievable." They never even tried to imagine themselves in Srebrenica in 1992 as having been attacked together with their families and friends without any food. Let's see what they would do. Perhaps they would manage to surprise themselves. In the indictment the Prosecution alleged that Oric's forces torched at least 50 villages and hamlets and described these in paragraph 932 of the Prosecution final trial brief. Your Honours, please take a look at the footnote, 1931, what exactly the Prosecution did to demonstrate the number of the villages in the footnote 1931. They listed individually each of the hamlets of the villages in the indictment as if each and every one of these was a separate village. So that every single hamlet of Kravica was treated as a separate village, including the hamlets of Jezestica and the same goes for Ratkovici. If you look at their list, then you will see that into these reportedly 50 villages they counted Glogova, you can see it here, it is a purely Muslim village, whose tragic fate is known to you. According to the Prosecution, here, Muslims torched their own Glogova and probably killed one another there. They also cited mixed villages among the torched villages, for instance, Magasici where it was in fact the Muslim houses that were torched. You will see that probably in order to achieve the necessary number of villages they mentioned Magasici three times, Dvorista three times, Kajici two times. They also cited Radijevici although the evidence showed that there was no torching there, even though, at the end of the Prosecution case, these charges in relation to Radijevici were dismissed. Although they separated these villages into hamlets, they weren't able to achieve the number of 50 villages, not even remotely. Not to speak of what they haven't managed to prove in regard with the torching, they haven't been able to prove the pattern as well as many other things. The Prosecution argues that Oric himself agreed that various communication means existed in his interview. This is something that they expounded in their reply to our final trial brief. Your Honours, please take a look at that reply and look at paragraph 106 and footnote 199. In trying to establish what it was that Oric in fact stated in this part of the interview, you will encounter great difficulties because none of what they allege is written there is in fact to be found. Also, in paragraph 112, footnote 212, out of nine references, six contain nothing whatsoever that would serve to confirm their allegation that Oric described the way communication means were used. I can now read out to you the footnotes although it would take too much time. The same goes for paragraph 113 and footnote 216. Paragraph 113, footnote 216. Let us take a look at what Oric said indeed as regards means of communication. Your Honours, you will see that while I'll be speaking that I will mention some names on the following slide that do not appear in the English. For example, something said by Nijaz Masic or Nedzad. It is not a mistake on my part but, rather, those are examples of how the Prosecutor adjusted the translation and left out some portions. To go back to what Oric said regarding communication, you have the interview reference. Investigator: "Now, to clarify a few things before I ask you something in general, as concerns communication during the period of war, that is from 1992 until the demilitarisation, the way you communicated with your other commanders, as well as with Sarajevo and Tuzla consisted of the following, couriers; is that correct? "Answer: Yes. "Question: Ham radios? "Answer: Yes. "Question: And the fax you told us about yesterday? "Answer: For a very short time, very short time. Until August. And Masic said that therefore it was at the very beginning. Later on we didn't have it. "Question: Was there any other sort of communication apart from the aforementioned three?" I apologise to the interpreters, but what was written here in Bosnian is something I can hardly read. I believe they will understand. "Question: And was there any other communication or types of communication apart from those three? "Answer: But you don't have the packet communication there. "Question: So that would be the fourth? "Answer: No, but I told you about this. "Question: You did. "Answer: And that's what arrived just prior to the demilitarisation. And since Nedzad was working there they sent that from Tuzla in order to wire-tap the Chetniks. That's what I said. "Question: So those were the four ways? "Answer: As for the couriers -- "Question: No need to go into that. "Answer: No, no. It had nothing to do with Sarajevo and Tuzla at the beginning." Your Honours, this was another type of questioning that the international Prosecutor shouldn't be proud of, because the way it was acquired runs contrary to the basic postulates of criminal procedure. The investigators did not allow Oric to explain certain facts important for his potential criminal liability. Apart from -- instead of allowing him to do that, he was interrupted aggressively, and they claimed he said something he never did. Although he denied two out of the four means of communication they cited, the investigator said, "So those were the four." And on the basis of that, they carried on with their interview. Apart -- instead of being ashamed and putting such evidence deep underground, away from the eyes of the public, they invoke such evidence and seek a conviction on the basis of evidence acquired in such a way. They paid a lot of attention to the allegedly existing system of couriers to support their thesis that Oric, probably via the couriers as one of the means of communication, realised effective control over his subordinates in the besieged Muslim villages. If one is to look at what Oric said concerning this type of communication with other groups in the field, you will find that he described very basic communication with other groups pertaining to danger warnings only. They also dealt with urgent requests for assistance, for example, in food, medication, ammunition, and so on and so forth. And this was confirmed by all of the Defence witnesses. This only points to a certain type of coordination in the very broad sense of the word. This is no communication that would enable any commander in the world to have effective control. The Prosecutor will immediately try to convince you that coordination was one of the command principles in the General Staff of the SFRY doctrine and Oric used it. The principle of command laid out in the doctrine of the General Staff of the SFRY. In their final brief in paragraph 283, they show you a provision that in true fact corresponds to the level of the corps commander, who is duty-bound to organise coordination and control to implement his decisions. There was no corps in Srebrenica. There was no corps commander. And the rules of the SFRY General Staff do not prescribe that the provisions pertaining to the corps should be applied to staffs, and such SFRY rules were not in place in Srebrenica and people there were not familiar with them. It is unbelievable how the Prosecutor tried to distort evidence, rules, Oric's interview, as well as witness testimonies. In their reply, paragraph 107, footnote 202, they stated that Muslim soldiers had come up with a way to charge their radio in order for it to be used to communicate in the military sense of the word and they relied for that on one of the Defence witnesses, Suad Smajlovic. Your Honours, Smajlovic never even came close to mention anything like that. He mentioned the way they charged their radio transistors. They used to listen to the Serb news and the Serb media. He did not have any sort of military communication in mind for charging such radio stations. Oric's interview, as well as other evidence, show that it's the same basic type of communication in the period relevant to the indictment existed between Srebrenica, Sarajevo and Tuzla, no matter how hard the Prosecutor tried to show the contrary. All Oric's contacts boil down to assistance -- requests for assistance, and that's that. There was no other type of reporting in the sense of superior/subordinate relationship in the period relevant to the indictment. Your Honours, perhaps this would be a good time for me to stop, and I will continue briefly tomorrow. After that, my colleague will address the counts of detention and as well as applicable law.
